statedGuarantee: An unprivileged Linux process sandbox for code an AI agent executes on a developer workstation. Policy is split by enforcement point: static, input-independent policy (readable/writable path prefixes, denied paths, TCP ports, IPC scope, unconditional syscall denials) is compiled into Landlock (ABI 6+, Linux 6.12+) and seccomp-bpf and enforced by the kernel with no supervisor in the loop; runtime-dependent decisions (resolved connect destination, execve argv, HTTP method/host/path, filesystem effects to be captured rather than applied) are routed to a narrow seccomp-user-notification supervisor in the trusted parent, which replies Allow/Deny(errno) or performs the operation on-behalf via pidfd_getfd. Confinement requires no root, no cgroups, no image, and no mandatory namespaces, is installed after fork() with PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS before exec, and is therefore inherited by the whole confined process tree. A pipeline operator composes stages with heterogeneous confinements so that capability separation (private-data access vs. network vs. exposure to untrusted content) is enforced by the kernel across process trees. Filesystem effects are reversible via two unprivileged copy-on-write backends (commit / abort / dry-run). Where neither layer can decide soundly, the policy fails closed.
advertisedRhetoric: "static, input-independent policy is compiled into kernel-enforced rules, while a narrow supervisor handles runtime-dependent decisions and virtualized effects"; the pipeline gives capability separation "enforced by the kernel rather than trusted to the LLM’s judgment"; and against prompt injection Sandlock "provides an unprivileged, kernel-enforced substrate on which the separated stages run". Landlock is called "the kernel-enforced “static” layer of policy". Notably the paper does NOT overclaim: it repeatedly names what is not a boundary (argv matching, pipe content, cooperative resource caps) and declares kernel bugs, side channels and privileged local attackers out of scope.
tierSpan: If a decision is known before execve, Sandlock compiles it into Landlock or seccomp-bpf so the kernel enforces it without supervisor involvement.
cheapestDefeat: Work entirely inside the granted policy; the kernel boundary is never touched. Two concrete routes. (1) Exfiltrate through an allowlisted endpoint. The endpoint allowlist is per-destination, not per-payload, and the paper itself states the gap: an agent that legitimately reaches api.openai.com:443 can carry attacker-chosen bytes to that same allowed IP. The intended answer (HTTP method/host/path rules) requires the workload to trust an injected sandbox CA; adversarial code simply speaks raw TLS to the allowlisted destination, and then, in the paper's own words, "TLS flows are governed only by endpoint policy". No privilege, no race, no kernel bug. (2) Use the scratch grant the system's own compatibility guidance recommends: "The main tuning is to grant each tool its temporary directories (e.g. /tmp for compiler intermediates, /dev/null)." A writable /tmp granted to more than one stage is a shared writable channel and a drop point for executables, widening the policy by configuration rather than by attack. Actually breaking the boundary (as opposed to living within it) requires a Landlock/seccomp/kernel vulnerability, an over-broad grant, or defeat of the ptrace-based freeze used for argv reads — and the first is explicitly declared out of scope, which is why the mechanism itself scores T2 rather than lower. Cheapest defeat of the SUPERVISOR-decided sub-guarantees is lower still: argv-based gating is self-declared evadable by renaming or reimplementing a binary, and CLONE_THREAD is excluded from the process counter, so unbounded threads evade the process cap.
placementSpan: We assume the sandboxed process may execute attacker-influenced code or consume attacker-controlled data, including package scripts, downloaded files, tool outputs, and generated commands. The host kernel, the Sandlock supervisor, and the embedding agent runtime are trusted; kernel vulnerabilities, side channels, privileged local attackers, and deliberate exhaustion of global kernel resources are out of scope.

coverageSpans.E1: Sandlock uses it for constraints whose verdict is independent of syscall-time data: filesystem read/write scope, TCP port scope, and IPC boundaries.
coverageSpans.E1_eval: Reads and writes outside the granted scope are denied while in-scope access succeeds
coverageSpans.E2: Argv inspection is an observation and policy-tightening signal, not a containment boundary: matching a binary name cannot stop adversarial code, which can rename or reimplement the tool.
coverageSpans.E2_counting: Fork-like syscalls are gated by a counter; thread creation (CLONE_THREAD) is excluded, and excess processes receive EAGAIN.
coverageSpans.E3: Allowlisting at the IP/port layer is necessary but not sufficient: a model that legitimately calls api.openai.com:443 can also call attacker-controlled endpoints through the same allowed IP.
coverageSpans.E3_https: HTTPS inspection is opt-in because it requires the workload to trust a sandbox CA; otherwise TLS flows are governed only by endpoint policy.
coverageSpans.E4: a connect to a host outside the endpoint allowlist is refused while an allowlisted endpoint connects
coverageSpans.E4_pinning: Concrete hostnames are resolved once at sandbox start and pinned for the child process, eliminating DNS-rebinding attacks.
coverageSpans.E5: An npm install step legitimately needs network access and writes under node_modules that the test step it sets up should not retain
coverageSpans.E6: Sandboxes run alongside the developer’s editor, SSH keys, and source trees. Confinement must be unprivileged (developer accounts rarely have free use of sudo) and must default-deny the rest of the home directory.
coverageSpans.E7: A pipeline is a sequence of stages connected by pipes; each stage has its own filesystem, network, resource, and runtime policy.
coverageSpans.E7_limit: sound decompositions remain the author’s responsibility: Sandlock kernel-enforces the separation specified, but does not prove that the untrusted-content stage never needs network or that the networked stage never needs private data.

schneider.surrogate: A per-stage, kernel-enforced capability bound that is a genuine safety property and exactly what a reference monitor enforces: no filesystem operation outside the granted read/write path scope, no connect to a destination outside the once-resolved endpoint allowlist, no IPC outside the Landlock IPC scope, no syscall in the seccomp deny set, and (cooperatively) no more than N processes. Landlock and seccomp-bpf ARE the monitor, in-kernel and inherited by the whole process tree.
schneider.objective: Prompt-injection resistance / the “lethal trifecta” objective the pipeline operator is motivated by: that private data reached by one stage does not flow to an external party, i.e. non-interference between a private-data source and a network sink. That is an information-flow hyperproperty, not a safety property of a single execution, and no monitor over one run can enforce it. The paper is explicit that it does not achieve it — "Sandlock bounds stage capabilities, not pipe content: a compromised upstream stage can still shape bytes consumed downstream" — and defers to complementary data-provenance defenses (CaMeL). The split is stated honestly rather than elided, which is unusual for this corpus.

notes:
FULL TEXT read from the arXiv HTML (v1, LaTeXML render), all nine sections plus both tables and the effectiveness table; not coded from the abstract. Workshop paper (Agentic OS Workshop, ASPLOS 2026), self-described "Preliminary Evaluation". Authors: Cong Wang (Multikernel Technologies), Yusheng Zheng (UC Santa Cruz). Code at github.com/multikernel/sandlock (not inspected — grade is from the paper only).

TIER, WORKED EXPLICITLY. Guarantee: a confined process and every descendant cannot touch the filesystem outside the granted scope, cannot reach an endpoint outside the resolved allowlist, and cannot make a denied syscall. Mechanism that must fail: the Landlock domain plus the seccomp-bpf filter, both installed after fork() with PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS set before exec, therefore inherited across fork and preserved across execve and never loosenable by the child. Cheapest adversary action causing that failure: a Landlock/seccomp/kernel vulnerability, or an over-broad grant by the operator. That action defeats an OS mechanism, so T2. This is a genuine T2 and a defensible anchor for the corpus — unlike proxy/hook designs, there is no path that simply does not traverse the chokepoint, because the chokepoint is a kernel LSM domain and a kernel BPF filter rather than an in-process interposer. The seccomp-notification supervisor does NOT drop the score to T3: the child cannot decline to trap, since the kernel forces the notification, and the design fails closed ("If neither layer can enforce the policy without a race or a semantic mismatch, Sandlock denies the operation rather than silently weakening the policy"), with SECCOMP_IOCTL_NOTIF_ID_VALID bracketing and no use of Continue on the held syscalls, so the classic Garfinkel argument-race bypass is addressed rather than hand-waved.

WHERE I DEPART FROM THE HEADLINE TIER. Two named sub-guarantees are genuinely weaker than T2 and an adjudicator must not let the T2 headline launder them. (a) HTTP method/host/path access control is a local proxy the supervisor redirects flows into — a T3 chokepoint — and over HTTPS it holds only if the workload trusts an injected sandbox CA; without that, the paper says TLS is governed by endpoint policy alone. Table 1's own footnote concedes this. (b) policy_fn/argv gating is declared by the authors themselves to be an observation signal and NOT a containment boundary. (c) Resource caps are "enforced cooperatively via syscall interception rather than at allocation time inside the kernel", with the memory bound on requested address space, not resident pages. I scored the overall tier on the fs/net/IPC/syscall spine (T2) because that is the paper's central claim, and recorded the weaker sub-guarantees here and in the coverage cells. A stricter coder could score the whole entry T3 on the strength of (a); I judged that would misrepresent the spine, but flag it as the single largest judgment call in this coding.

COVERAGE REASONING. E1 is the only "covered" cell, and it is the strongest cell in the corpus so far: Landlock filesystem scope is default-deny, kernel-enforced, inherited by every descendant with no way to widen it, applies to undeclared paths by construction, covers rename and unlink (renameat2/unlinkat also appear in the supervisor table for COW capture, but the boundary is Landlock, not the supervisor), and the effectiveness table behaviorally confirms both deny and allow directions. Sandlock also closes inherited descriptors ("close fds 3+") before exec, removing the usual inherited-fd escape. Residual doubt I could not resolve from the text and which keeps this from being airtight: the paper never enumerates the seccomp deny set, so whether ptrace, process_vm_writev or /proc/pid/mem write paths are blocked is unstated — and Sandlock itself uses ptrace for its freeze, so ptrace is clearly not universally denied to the parent. I still coded covered because those are write channels into other processes rather than filesystem writes, and Landlock ABI 6 scopes signals and abstract sockets.

E2 partial: descendant spawns ARE mediated (the inherited seccomp filter traps clone/fork/vfork/clone3 from any descendant, and children are registered via a traced ptrace creation event before user code runs), so the depth rule is satisfied — but coverage of every instance is not. CLONE_THREAD is explicitly excluded from the counter, so unbounded thread creation evades the cap; and spawn-by-identity cannot be enforced at all because the authors state argv matching is evadable. Ceiling is partial.

E3 partial by the covert-channel rule, not by the depth rule. Depth is fine — descendant egress traps through the inherited filter and the Landlock net domain. But the stated contract explicitly excludes the channel through which egress-as-exfiltration is achieved: an allowlisted endpoint carries arbitrary payload, and the paper names this exact scenario in its own motivation. Honesty about the gap does not close it. Also unproven: only TCP, UDP and ICMP are named in the endpoint model, so other socket families (e.g. AF_PACKET) have no stated treatment; and Landlock covers TCP connect/bind but not UDP/ICMP, which fall back to the supervisor.

E4 partial is INCIDENTAL coverage and should be read that way — the paper never mentions VCS, git, or push. I did not code not-covered because the guarantee genuinely reaches the effector: a push to a non-allowlisted forge is refused by the endpoint allowlist (behaviorally tested as the generic non-allowlisted-connect row), and credentials for the push are subject to the default-deny filesystem scope. But once a forge host is allowlisted there is zero ref, repo, or branch granularity, so it provably fails to reach other instances. Adjudicator may reasonably prefer not-covered here; I flag it as my second-largest judgment call.

E5 partial: this is the paper's own motivating workload (npm install, curl | sh, package registry access) and install hooks running as descendants inherit the identical kernel confinement — so hooks AND their network activity are mediated at the same tier as the parent, which is what the depth rule demands. It falls short of covered for the same reason as E3: a hook egressing to an allowlisted registry is unconstrained in payload. Note also that COW capture makes hook filesystem writes REVERSIBLE (commit/abort/dry-run), which is a real and unusual property for this effector, but reversibility is not prevention. No install-hook case appears in the ten effectiveness checks, so evidence for E5 specifically is weaker than L2.

E6 partial, capped by rule: there is NO published credential list anywhere in the paper. File-backed credentials are handled well (default-deny on the rest of the home directory, ~/.ssh named in the threat model, an explicit deny_path("/etc/shadow") example) and cloud metadata endpoints are blocked by default-deny endpoint allowlisting with hostnames pinned at start. But environment variables are never mentioned in the entire paper — no scrubbing, no filtering — and the confined child is fork/exec'd from the trusted parent, so it inherits the parent's environment, API keys included. Keychain/agent sockets get no named treatment beyond generic Landlock IPC scoping. So: strong on paths, silent on env, undefined list → partial.

E7 partial, and this was the closest call in the coding. Sandlock has no notion of agent identity, delegation, or a sub-agent principal, and a remotely dispatched sub-agent (an MCP call, a model API call) is invisible to it — that argues for not-covered. What kept it at partial: the guarantee does reach some instances. A locally spawned sub-agent inherits a Landlock domain it can only tighten, never widen, so a sub-agent provably cannot exceed its parent's capabilities — monotonic capability inheritance, kernel-enforced. And the pipeline operator gives author-declared stages genuinely distinct, kernel-enforced capability sets, explicitly framed for the planner/executor split. What it does not do: let a RUNNING agent spawn a new stage with a new bounded capability set (pipelines are composed by the trusted host before the run, not by the workload), and it does not verify the decomposition is sound.

EVIDENCE L2: Table 3 reports ten deterministic deny/allow checks actually executed against the system with observed outcomes recorded, and "All ten checks behaved as the policy requires." That is behavioral confirmation, not claim-only. It is NOT L3 — no reproducible bypass is presented, and importantly there is no adversarial evaluation at all: the ten checks are benign, direct, single-syscall attempts, with no attempt to reach a denied resource by an alternative syscall, an inherited descriptor, a symlink, a renamed binary, or a thread-based evasion of the process cap. The paper concedes "A systematic compatibility study across the long tail of agent tooling is future work." Performance numbers (~5 ms startup, Redis within noise, ~1,900 COW forks/s) are median-of-N on a single AMD Ryzen 5 5500U workstation, Linux 6.18 — single-machine, no variance analysis beyond error bars, and Docker is benchmarked rootful while Table 1 compares features against rootless Docker (the authors disclose this asymmetry).

CORPUS PLACEMENT. This is the cleanest T2 anchor available: unprivileged, no root, no namespaces required, kernel-enforced, descendant-inheriting, fails closed, and with an author-stated boundary between what is enforced and what is merely observed. Its value to the SoK is precisely as the contrast case — it shows what T2 buys (E1 covered, real descendant depth on E2/E3/E5) and, by its own admission, what T2 still cannot buy (payload-level egress control without a CA, information-flow objectives, any notion of an agent principal). Use the Schneider split here as the model of an honestly declared surrogate/objective gap.
